summary: Aegis Health is an offline-first astronaut health companion for missions with limited connectivity. The crew app enables routine check-ins, guided measurements, personal-baseline comparisons, reminders, action recommendations, and an Emergency Quick Action flow. It focuses on sleep, heart signals, hydration, mood, activity, radiation exposure, symptoms, and mission-relevant indicators, while clearly showing uncertainty, data quality, and provenance. The future mission-control web console lets medical and mission personnel review trends, evidence, escalations, acknowledgments, and synchronization history. The system uses encrypted local storage, scheduled notifications, explicit sync states, versioned records, and human-review safeguards. NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources provide contextual evidence rather than invented diagnostic thresholds. A phased roadmap begins with shared data contracts and an offline app shell, then adds measurements, routines, mission modes, evidence, console capabilities, hardware integrations, and validation. The initial demonstration follows an astronaut on Mars transit managing gradual recovery drift and an urgent simulated symptom event offline.
details:
Purpose

We are developing Aegis Health as an astronaut health and mission-monitoring prototype. Our purpose is to bring physiological and environmental readings onto a local touchscreen and a website, with a private mission record for each astronaut account.

What does this do?

Our proposed system receives measurements from connected sensors, presents available readings on an ESP32-driven 3.5-inch touchscreen, and sends data over USB to a Windows computer. The website can collect these readings into an active mission, preserve their timestamps, and produce observational reports.

Radiation monitoring

The Geiger module detects ionizing-radiation events. Our firmware counts these events over a rolling 60-second window and displays the result in counts per minute (CPM). This provides a record of detected radiation counts alongside other mission readings. Converting counts to a personal dose or dose rate requires detector calibration and information about the radiation field.

Heart rate and atmospheric CO2

Our optical sensor supplies a pulse signal for an experimental heart-rate estimate. The CO2 sensor measures atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration in parts per million (ppm). The local display and Windows console present these readings, while the website can save them as mission data.

Additional connected devices

The website also accepts oxygen saturation, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature, respiration rate, and ECG, optical-pulse or respiratory waveform samples when compatible acquisition hardware supplies them through the supported data format. Each measurement needs its appropriate sensor or instrument. The included optical, CO2 and Geiger modules provide the measurements described above.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Aegis Health helps astronauts manage their health independently while reducing reliance on continuous communication with Earth. It supports early recognition of concerning changes, encourages healthy routines, reduces alert fatigue, and preserves a reliable record of health events during offline periods. The intended impact is to improve crew safety, support faster and better-informed medical review, and make health monitoring practical during long-duration missions to the Moon or Mars.

The system is designed as decision support rather than a diagnostic tool. It uses personal baselines, repeated measurements, data-quality indicators, uncertainty labels, and human oversight instead of presenting unexplained risk scores or unsupported medical conclusions.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

The existing demonstration surface is a React-based web application intended to serve as a mission-control dashboard and browser demonstration. The planned crew application uses React Native and Expo, with TypeScript shared across the mobile app and web console. Local SQLite or an equivalent encrypted database stores measurements, check-ins, routines, emergency events, evidence summaries, and pending synchronization records. Local notifications support scheduled check-ins and mission routines.

The first implementation can use manual data entry and simulated telemetry. Future versions may connect validated wearable devices, medical sensors, or other approved data sources through common adapter interfaces. A synchronization service and server-side database will support authorized mission-control review, role-based access, audit history, and conflict resolution.

Creativity and Design Considerations

The project is creative because it combines astronaut self-care, offline-first software, explainable decision support, mission-environment awareness, and NASA evidence in one coordinated experience. Rather than treating health as a single score, it connects measurements to understandable actions and personal trends. Its interactive body and system map can help non-medical users explore how different spaceflight hazards relate to body systems.

The team considered five major spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments. Additional considerations included communication delays, accessibility, privacy, data security, notification fatigue, uncertain or incomplete measurements, role-based permissions, emergency escalation, and the differences between operational telemetry, self-reported information, clinical measurements, and research evidence.

NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources provide scientific context, but the project avoids inventing diagnostic thresholds or turning research findings into individual medical advice. The design also ensures that astronauts can continue using essential features offline and that every recommendation remains explainable, traceable, and subject to qualified human review.
